claims.source: Therefore, although the m1G37 modification is present in ASLPro, the shift in the +1 frame can still occur.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of the +1 frame in the crystal structure with m1G37 present.

claims.claim: The presence of a near-cognate, slippery codon is sufficient to promote a +1 mRNA frameshift.
claims.source: These data indicate that the presence of a near-cognate, slippery codon is sufficient to promote a +1 mRNA frameshift.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing +1 frameshifting with m1G37 present.

claims.claim: Biochemical studies of other near-cognate mRNA-tRNA pairs in the P site show frameshifting in both directions on the mRNA.
claims.source: Consistent with our observations, biochemical studies of other near-cognate mRNA-tRNA pairs in the P site also show frameshifting in both directions on the mRNA (Zaher and Green, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zaher and Green, 2009.

claims.claim: A structure of tRNAPro-CGG containing the m1G37 modification bound to a cognate CCG codon in the ribosomal P site was solved to a resolution of 3.2 Å.
claims.source: As a control, we solved a structure of tRNAPro-CGG containing the m1G37 modification bound to a cognate CCG codon in the ribosomal P site to a resolution of 3.2 Å (Figure 2A and Table 3 and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: tRNAPro-CGG containing m1G37 bound to a cognate CCG codon binds in the classical P/P state.
claims.source: tRNAPro-CGG binds in the classical P/P state (bound to the P site on the 50S and the 30S subunits) and interacts with the proline codon in the 0 frame.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claims.claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG with m1G37 bound to a cognate CCG codon, the G36-G35-C34 anticodon nucleotides form three Watson–Crick base-pairs with the C+1-C+2-G+3 proline codon nucleotides.
claims.source: Specifically, the G36-G35-C34 anticodon nucleotides form three Watson–Crick base-pairs with the C+1-C+2-G+3 proline codon nucleotides, respectively (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The methyl group at position 1 of the nucleobase of G37 stacks with the nucleobase of anticodon nucleotide G36 to form a canonical four-nucleotide stack between nucleotides 34–37.
claims.source: The methyl group at position 1 of the nucleobase of G37 stacks with the nucleobase of anticodon nucleotide G36 to form a canonical four-nucleotide stack between nucleotides 34–37.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The anticodon stack is important for productive interactions with both mRNA and the ribosome.
claims.source: This anticodon stack is important for productive interactions with both mRNA and the ribosome (Maehigashi et al., 2014; Grosjean et al., 1976; Gustilo et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maehigashi et al., 2014; Grosjean et al., 1976; Gustilo et al., 2008.

claims.claim: tRNAPro isoacceptors do not appear to spontaneously move into the +1 frame on non-slippery codons.
claims.source: The P/P location of tRNAPro-CGG is thus consistent with functional assays demonstrating that tRNAPro isoacceptors do not appear to spontaneously move into the +1 frame on non-slippery codons (Björk et al., 1989; Gamper et al., 2015a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Björk et al., 1989; Gamper et al., 2015a.

claims.claim: A 3.9 Å structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking the m1G37 modification (G37 Δm1) and interacting with a cognate CCG proline codon in the P site was solved.
claims.source: We next solved a 3.9 Å structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking the m1G37 modification (G37 Δm1) and interacting with a cognate CCG proline codon in the P site (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D and Table 3 and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a cognate CCG codon adopts a P/P orientation.
claims.source: Although the m1G37 modification was previously shown to be critical for high-affinity binding and decoding of the cognate CCG codon at the A site (Nguyen et al., 2019), its influence on the overall conformation of tRNAPro-CGG in the P site appears to be minimal as the tRNA adopts a P/P orientation (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a cognate CCG codon, the mRNA remains in the 0 frame with three Watson–Crick base-pair interactions between the codon and the anticodon.
claims.source: Notably, the mRNA remains in the 0 frame with three Watson–Crick base-pair interactions between the codon and the anticodon (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The absence of the m1G37 modification correlates with a slightly weaker U32-A38 pairing when compared to modified tRNAPro-CGG.
claims.source: The absence of the m1G37 modification correlates with a slightly weaker U32-A38 pairing when compared to modified tRNAPro-CGG (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: tRNAPro-GGG lacking m1G37 on a non-slippery codon remained in the 0 frame according to toeprint analyses.
claims.source: This observation is also consistent with toeprint analyses demonstrating that tRNAPro-GGG lacking m1G37 on a non-slippery codon remained in the 0 frame (Gamper et al., 2015a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gamper et al., 2015a.

claims.claim: A ribosome structure of tRNAPro-CGG with m1G37 bound to a +1 slippery CCC-U codon in the P site was solved to a resolution of 3.2 Å.
claims.source: In an attempt to reconcile the exact role of the m1G37 modification in tRNAPro-CGG in the context of a +1 slippery CCC-U codon, we next solved a ribosome structure of this complex in the P site to a resolution of 3.2 Å (Figure 2C and Table 3 and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: tRNAPro-CGG with m1G37 bound to a slippery CCC-U codon moves from the P site towards the E site, adopting a position referred to as e*/E.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, tRNAPro-CGG moves from the P site towards the E site, adopting a position on the ribosome which we refer to as e*/E (Hong et al., 2018) (where e* signifies an intermediate position between the 30S subunit P and the E sites and E signifies a 50S E-site position) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The e*/E position of tRNAPro-CGG when bound to a slippery codon is different from the classical P/P position that the same tRNA adopts when it interacts with a cognate CCG codon.
claims.source: The e*/E position of tRNAPro-CGG when bound to this slippery codon is different from the classical P/P position that the same tRNA adopts when it interacts with a cognate CCG codon (compare Figure 2A with Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by comparing the crystal structures shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claims.claim: The ability of tRNAPro-CGG to move towards the E site when bound to a slippery proline codon suggests that it is this near-cognate codon–anticodon interaction alone that is sufficient to destabilize tRNAPro-CGG.
claims.source: Therefore, the ability of tRNAPro-CGG to move towards the E site when bound to a slippery proline codon suggests that it is this near-cognate codon–anticodon interaction alone that is sufficient to destabilize tRNAPro-CGG (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claims.claim: The e*/E position of the tRNAPro-CGG-mRNA pair is coupled to large conformational changes of the 30S head domain.
claims.source: The e*/E position of the tRNAPro-CGG-mRNA pair is additionally coupled to large conformational changes of the 30S head domain (Figure 3 and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The 30S head domain swivels in a ~18° counterclockwise direction while also undergoing a ~5° tilt away from the ribosome and perpendicular to the mRNA path in the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure.
claims.source: The head domain swivels in a ~18° counterclockwise direction while also undergoing a ~5° tilt away from the ribosome and perpendicular to the mRNA path (Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure and compared to reference structures.

claims.claim: The head domain is comprised of 16S rRNA nucleotides 930–1380 and seven ribosomal proteins (S3, S7, S9, S10, S13, S14, and S19).
claims.source: The head domain is comprised of 16S rRNA nucleotides 930–1380 and seven ribosomal proteins (S3, S7, S9, S10, S13, S14, and S19) (Belardinelli et al., 2016a; Guo and Noller, 2012)
claims.evidence: This is a structural definition supported by citations to Belardinelli et al., 2016a; Guo and Noller, 2012.

claims.claim: The head domain moves as a rigid body during EF-G-mediated translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pairs on the 30S.
claims.source: The head domain is comprised of 16S rRNA nucleotides 930–1380 and seven ribosomal proteins (S3, S7, S9, S10, S13, S14, and S19) (Belardinelli et al., 2016a; Guo and Noller, 2012) that collectively move as a rigid body during EF-G-mediated translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pairs on the 30S (Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The swivel and tilting of the head domain of e*/E tRNAPro-CGG occurs in the absence of EF-G.
claims.source: The same swivel and tilting of the head domain of e*/E tRNAPro-CGG occurs but our structure lacks EF-G.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure which does not contain EF-G.

claims.claim: Even with the m1G37 modification, interactions of tRNAPro-CGG with the P site are destabilized when bound to a near-cognate codon, promoting its movement toward the E site along with 30S head domain swivel and tilting.
claims.source: This result indicates that even with the m1G37 modification, interactions of tRNAPro-CGG with the P site are destabilized when bound to a near-cognate codon, promoting its movement toward the E site along with 30S head domain swivel and tilting.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claims.claim: The ribosome interacts extensively with the mRNA in the A site to ensure accurate decoding but interacts less substantially with the P-site codon, while the E-site mRNA codon is the least monitored.
claims.source: The ribosome interacts extensively with the mRNA in the A site to ensure accurate decoding but interacts less substantially with the P-site codon, while the E-site mRNA codon is the least monitored.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ribosome function.

claims.claim: The ribosome interacts with E-site mRNA at two positions through non-sequence-specific contacts: 16S rRNA nucleotide G693 stacks with the first nucleotide of the E-site mRNA codon and the G926 nucleobase contacts the phosphate of the third mRNA codon nucleotide.
claims.source: The ribosome interacts with E-site mRNA at two positions through non-sequence-specific contacts: 16S rRNA nucleotide G693 stacks with the first nucleotide of the E-site mRNA codon and the G926 nucleobase contacts the phosphate of the third mRNA codon nucleotide (Figure 4B and C; Selmer et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Selmer et al., 2006 and shown in Figures 4B and C.

claims.claim: The e* position of tRNAPro-CGG signifies that the tRNA is closer to the E site than the P site on the 30S.
claims.source: The e* position of tRNAPro-CGG signifies that the tRNA is closer to the E site than the P site on the 30S, however it is similar to the pe/E tRNA position seen in translocation intermediate ribosome structures containing EF-G (Figure 4D; Zhou et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with translocation intermediate structures.

claims.claim: Only two nucleotides of the codon–anticodon interaction of the pe/E tRNA are positioned in the E site leaving a pocket for an additional nucleotide to occupy upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair.
claims.source: Only two nucleotides of the codon–anticodon interaction of the pe/E tRNA are positioned in the E site leaving a pocket for an additional nucleotide to occupy upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair (Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014) (compare Figure 4C with Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In the structure containing an e*/E tRNAPro-CGG bound to a near-cognate, slippery codon, the first three nucleotides of the codon fully occupy the E site.
claims.source: In our structure containing an e*/E tRNAPro-CGG bound to a near-cognate, slippery codon, the first three nucleotides of the codon fully occupy the E site (Figure 4E), despite the codon–anticodon adopting an intermediate position on the 30S between the P and the E sites.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The compaction of the mRNA in the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure means there is no space for the entire four-nucleotide codon in the E site upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair.
claims.source: This compaction of the mRNA means there is no space for the entire four-nucleotide codon in the E site upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claims.claim: The mRNA path 5' from the E site turns sharply by ~100° as the mRNA transits to the outside of the ribosome.
claims.source: Additionally, the mRNA path 5' from the E site turns sharply by ~100° as the mRNA transits to the outside of the ribosome (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Upon full translocation of the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG to the E site, the first nucleotide of the codon would be displaced from the E site to accommodate the three-nucleotide codon or the last three nucleotides of the CCC-U codon, positioning the mRNA in the +1 frame.
claims.source: In the case of e*/E tRNAPro-CGG, upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair to the E site, the first nucleotide of the codon would be displaced from the E site to accommodate the three-nucleotide codon or the last three nucleotides of the CCC-U codon. This placement would position the mRNA in the +1 frame.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation and the constraints of the E site.

claims.claim: The ribosome minimally interacts with the mRNA-tRNA pair in the P site: 16S rRNA C1400 contacts G966 and stacks with the third base-pair of the codon–anticodon.
claims.source: The ribosome minimally interacts with the mRNA-tRNA pair in the P site: 16S rRNA C1400 contacts G966 and stacks with the third base-pair of the codon–anticodon (Figure 5A; Selmer et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Selmer et al., 2006 and shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The G966-C1400 pair remains intact during translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair from the P to the E site as part of the head domain.
claims.source: The G966-C1400 pair remains intact during translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair from the P to the E site as part of the head domain, as evidenced by ribosome structures in translocation intermediate states containing EF-G (Figure 5B). (Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: In the structure containing e*/E tRNAPro-CGG bound to a CCC-U codon, the G966-C1400 interaction is ablated.
claims.source: In our structure containing e*/E tRNAPro-CGG bound to a CCC-U codon, the G966-C1400 interaction is ablated (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The disruption of the G966-C1400 interaction can be attributed to a dysregulation caused by the spontaneous translocation event.
claims.source: Since the G966-C1400 interaction is effectively the bridge between the head and body domains, this disruption can be attributed to a dysregulation caused by this spontaneous translocation event.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claims.claim: A 4.1 Å structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37(Δm1) and interacting with a near-cognate, slippery CCC-U codon at the P site was solved.
claims.source: Finally, we solved a 4.1 Å structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37(Δm1) and interacting with a near-cognate, slippery CCC-U codon at the P site.
claims.evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a CCC-U codon, the electron density for the majority of the tRNAPro-CGG on the 50S subunit is well-resolved, indicating that the tRNA has moved towards the E site on the 50S subunit.
claims.source: The electron density for the majority of the tRNAPro-CGG on the 50S subunit is well-resolved, indicating that, similar to the analogous structure solved in the presence of the m1G37 modification (Figure 2C), the tRNA has also moved towards the E site on the 50S subunit (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a CCC-U codon, the electron density is weak for the tRNAPro-CGG ASL and E-site mRNA indicating these regions are dynamic.
claims.source: In contrast, the electron density is weak for the tRNAPro-CGG ASL and E-site mRNA indicating these regions are dynamic in the context of slippery codon and in the absence of m1G37 modification (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claims.claim: Disordering of tRNAPro G37(Δm1) starts approximately at the beginning of the anticodon loop at nucleotides U32-A38.
claims.source: Disordering of tRNAPro G37(Δm1) starts approximately at the beginning of the anticodon loop at nucleotides U32-A38.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claims.claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a CCC-U codon, the 30S head domain region is disordered.
claims.source: Correspondingly, the 30S head domain region is also disordered (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), whereas the only region of the 30S body domain with poor electron density is the P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claims.claim: In the mRNA-tRNA pairing that causes high levels of frameshifting (tRNAPro lacking m1G37 on CCC-U codon), interactions with the tRNA are destabilized in the P site resulting in the codon–anticodon adopting an e* location and high mobility of the 30S head domain.
claims.source: Taken together, in this mRNA-tRNA pairing that causes high levels of frameshifting, interactions with the tRNA are destabilized in the P site resulting in the codon–anticodon adopting an e* location and high mobility of the 30S head domain.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claims.claim: The m1G37 modification in tRNAPro-CGG influences the overall stability of tRNAPro-CGG on the ribosome and causes large conformational changes between the tRNA and the 30S head domain.
claims.source: We find that this single methyl group influences the overall stability of tRNAPro-CGG on the ribosome in an unexpected manner and causes large conformational changes between the tRNA and the 30S head domain, a domain known to move extensively during translocation of the tRNAs (Wasserman et al., 2016; Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on the structural data presented.

claims.claim: The methylation of m1G37 alone does not stabilize tRNAPro-CGG on the ribosome; instead, its position is heavily influenced by interactions with a slippery proline codon.
claims.source: However, the methylation alone does not stabilize tRNAPro-CGG on the ribosome and, instead, its position is heavily influenced by interactions with a slippery proline codon.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on the structural data presented.

claims.claim: The location on the ribosome where frameshifting can occur is likely dependent on the type of frameshift (in the positive or negative direction on the mRNA) and whether tRNA or mRNA causes the frameshift.
claims.source: The location on the ribosome where frameshifting can occur is likely dependent on the type of frameshift (in the positive or negative directionon the mRNA) and whether tRNA or mRNA causes the frameshift (Dinman, 2012; Dunkle and Dunham, 2015; Atkins et al., 2016; Korniy et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dinman, 2012; Dunkle and Dunham, 2015; Atkins et al., 2016; Korniy et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The codon–anticodon interaction located in the 30S A site is strictly monitored by conserved 16S rRNA nucleotides to select for cognate tRNA.
claims.source: While the codon–anticodon interaction located in the 30S A site is strictly monitored by conserved 16S rRNA nucleotides to select for cognate tRNA (Ogle et al., 2002), there are comparatively few interactions with the codon–anticodon when positioned within the P and E sites, underscoring their different functional roles during the translation cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ogle et al., 2002.

claims.claim: There are comparatively few interactions with the codon–anticodon when positioned within the P and E sites.
claims.source: While the codon–anticodon interaction located in the 30S A site is strictly monitored by conserved 16S rRNA nucleotides to select for cognate tRNA (Ogle et al., 2002), there are comparatively few interactions with the codon–anticodon when positioned within the P and E sites, underscoring their different functional roles during the translation cycle.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ribosome function.

claims.claim: The relative absence of interactions in the P and E sites provides an opportunity for the mRNA to shift out of frame.
claims.source: The relative absence of interactions in the P and E sites provides an opportunity for the mRNA to shift out of frame.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claims.claim: Some tRNAPro isoacceptors frameshift either during translocation from the A to the P site or after the translocation step and once positioned in the P site.
claims.source: Some tRNAPro isoacceptors frameshift either during translocation from the A to the P site or after the translocation step and once positioned in the P site (Gamper et al., 2015a; Gamper et al., 2015b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gamper et al., 2015a; Gamper et al., 2015b.

claims.claim: Interactions with the P-site tRNA are limited to only 16S rRNA P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339 with the anticodon stem and 16S rRNA C1400 with the anticodon nucleotide 34.
claims.source: This frameshift is likely possible because interactions with the P-site tRNA are limited to only 16S rRNA P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339 with the anticodon stem and 16S rRNA C1400 with the anticodon nucleotide 34 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The P/E loop appears to indirectly enforce the mRNA frame by gripping the P-site tRNA.
claims.source: The P/E loop appears to indirectly enforce the mRNA frame by gripping the P-site tRNA and these interactions are maintained as the tRNA moves from the P site to a hybrid P/E state (Dunkle et al., 2011) and to a translocation intermediate pe/E state (Zhou et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and supported by citations to Dunkle et al., 2011 and Zhou et al., 2013.

claims.claim: In the structures of ASLPro interacting with the mRNA in the 0 frame, there is well-resolved density for G1338 and A1339.
claims.source: In the structures of ASLPro interacting with the mRNA in the 0 frame, there is well-resolved density for G1338 and A1339 (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,D, G), while there is some disordering of these nucleotides in the context of ASLPro bound to the near-cognate, slippery codon in the +1 frame (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, F and I).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures.

claims.claim: There is some disordering of G1338 and A1339 in the context of ASLPro bound to the near-cognate, slippery codon in the +1 frame.
claims.source: In the structures of ASLPro interacting with the mRNA in the 0 frame, there is well-resolved density for G1338 and A1339 (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,D, G), while there is some disordering of these nucleotides in the context of ASLPro bound to the near-cognate, slippery codon in the +1 frame (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, F and I).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures.

claims.claim: The inability for G1338 and A1339 to grip the anticodon stem when the codon–anticodon is in the +1 frame likely results in the destabilization of full-length tRNAPro in frameshift-competent contexts.
claims.source: The inability for G1338 and A1339 to grip the anticodon stem when the codon–anticodon is in the +1 frame likely results in the destabilization of full-length tRNAPro in these frameshift-competent contexts (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claims.claim: Simulations of the ribosome undergoing large movements of the head domain during translocation implicate nucleotides G1338 and A1339 in the coupling of 30S head dynamics and displacement of the P-site tRNA towards the E site.
claims.source: Simulations of the ribosome undergoing large movements of the head domain during translocation implicate nucleotides G1338 and A1339 in the coupling of 30S head dynamics and displacement of the P-site tRNA towards the E site (Nguyen and Whitford, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen and Whitford, 2016.

claims.claim: The lack of gripping by the P/E loop in the P site when a destabilized mRNA-tRNA interaction is present appears to bias tRNAPro toward the E site which, in turn, causes the 30S head domain to swivel and tilt as if EF-G were bound.
claims.source: Therefore, the lack of gripping by the P/E loop in the P site when a destabilized mRNA-tRNA interaction is present, appears to bias tRNAPro toward the E site which, in turn, causes the 30S head domain to swivel and tilt as if EF-G were bound.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claims.claim: 16S rRNA nucleotide G966 stacks with nucleotide 34 of the P-site tRNA anticodon.
claims.source: In addition to P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339, 16S rRNA nucleotide G966 is also part of the 30S head domain and stacks with nucleotide 34 of the P-site tRNA anticodon (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The 30S head is connected to the body domain via interactions of G966 with nucleotide C1400.
claims.source: The 30S head is connected to the body domain via interactions of G966 with nucleotide C1400; the G966-C1400 pair remains stacked beneath the P-site tRNA and follows the tRNA as it moves to a hybrid P/E state and to a translocation pe/E intermediate state upon EF-G binding (Figure 5B; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014; Dunkle et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014; Dunkle et al., 2011 and shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: In the case of P-site ASLPro interacting with a +1 slippery codon in the 0 or +1 frame, cis-Watson–Crick interactions form between C+3•C34 and U+4•C34, respectively.
claims.source: In the case of P-site ASLPro interacting with a +1 slippery codon in the 0 or +1 frame, cis-Watson–Crick interactions form between C+3•C34 and U+4•C34, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L.

claims.claim: Both the C+3•C34 and U+4•C34 interactions appear to result in reduced stacking with C1400.
claims.source: Both the C+3•C34 and U+4•C34 interactions appear to result in reduced stacking with C1400.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claims.claim: In structures of full-length tRNAPro-mRNA pairs that cause +1 frameshifting and destabilization at the P site, the G966-C1400 interaction is broken.
claims.source: In structures of full-length tRNAPro-mRNA pairs that cause +1 frameshifting and destabilization at the P site, the G966-C1400 interaction is broken (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The reduced interactions of G1338-A1339 and G966-C1400 with the tRNA appear to influence the movement of the P-site tRNA towards the E site.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest a connection between the reduced interactions of G1338-A1339 and G966-C1400 with the tRNA that appear to influence the movement of the P-site tRNA towards the E site.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claims.claim: Substitution of G966 substantially reduces ribosome activity to ~10% despite the mutation not being lethal.
claims.source: 16S rRNA nucleotides in the P site are generally more tolerable of mutations than the A-site 16S rRNA, although substitution of G966 substantially reduces ribosome activity to ~10% despite the mutation not being lethal (Abdi and Fredrick, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abdi and Fredrick, 2005.

claims.claim: The G966 mutant is suppressed by a G1338A mutation, indicating that the G1338A mutation can stabilize interactions with the P-site tRNA even in the absence of the C1400-G966 interaction.
claims.source: This G966 mutant is suppressed by a G1338A mutation, indicating that the G1338A mutation can stabilize interactions with the P-site tRNA even in the absence of the C1400-G966 interaction.

results.result: ASLPro bound to a slippery CCC-U codon in the P site can adopt both 0-frame and +1-frame conformations, demonstrating that the near-cognate codon-anticodon interaction alone is sufficient to promote frameshifting even in the presence of m1G37 modification.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C38 provide strong crystallographic evidence showing two distinct conformations in the asymmetric unit: one in the 0 frame (C30-C32) and one in the +1 frame (C33-C36). The structural data directly demonstrates that m1G37 presence does not prevent frameshifting when a slippery codon is present (C37-C38), supporting the conclusion that the codon context is critical.

results.result: Full-length tRNAPro-CGG with or without m1G37 modification bound to cognate CCG codons adopts a classical P/P state with the mRNA in the 0 frame, indicating that the absence of m1G37 alone does not destabilize tRNA in the P site on non-slippery codons.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C51 present crystallographic structures at 3.2 Å and 3.9 Å resolution showing that both modified and unmodified tRNAPro-CGG maintain P/P positioning on cognate codons (C41, C47-C48). The structural data is consistent with functional assays cited (C45, C51), providing converging evidence that m1G37 is not required for stability on cognate codons.

results.result: tRNAPro-CGG with m1G37 bound to a slippery CCC-U codon moves to an e*/E position coupled with large 30S head domain conformational changes (~18° swivel and ~5° tilt) in the absence of EF-G, demonstrating that the near-cognate codon-anticodon interaction destabilizes the tRNA even with the modification present.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C61 provide crystallographic evidence at 3.2 Å resolution showing the e*/E position (C53-C54) and quantified head domain movements (C57). The structural observations are well-documented with appropriate comparisons to EF-G-mediated translocation (C59-C60), supporting the conclusion that codon context drives destabilization independent of m1G37 presence.

results.result: tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a slippery CCC-U codon shows movement toward the E site on the 50S subunit but exhibits disorder in the anticodon stem-loop, E-site mRNA, and 30S head domain, indicating high mobility in this frameshifting-competent context.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 present a 4.1 Å structure showing differential electron density: well-resolved 50S-bound tRNA (C75) but disordered ASL, mRNA, and head domain (C76-C78). The disorder pattern is consistent with the interpretation of high mobility in frameshifting contexts (C79), though the lower resolution limits detailed structural analysis.

results.result: In the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure, the first three nucleotides of the four-nucleotide CCC-U codon fully occupy the E site despite the tRNA being in an intermediate position, creating spatial constraints that would require displacement of the first nucleotide upon full translocation, positioning the mRNA in the +1 frame.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C69 describe the mRNA path and E-site constraints based on structural observations (C66, C68) and comparisons with translocation intermediates (C64-C65). The inference about +1 frame positioning upon full translocation (C69) is logically derived from the spatial constraints observed in the structure, though it represents a prediction rather than direct observation.

results.result: The G966-C1400 interaction that bridges the 30S head and body domains is disrupted in the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure bound to a slippery codon, representing a dysregulation of the normal translocation process.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 document the G966-C1400 interaction in normal P-site binding (C70) and its maintenance during EF-G-mediated translocation (C71), then show its disruption in the frameshifting context (C72). The structural evidence directly supports the conclusion of dysregulation (C73), consistent with the spontaneous translocation observed.

results.result: The P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339 show well-resolved density when ASLPro is in the 0 frame but disorder in the +1 frame, suggesting that the inability of these nucleotides to grip the anticodon stem in frameshifting contexts contributes to tRNA destabilization and biases movement toward the E site.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 present electron density observations (C89-C90) showing differential ordering of P/E loop nucleotides depending on frame. The inference about P/E loop gripping and its role in destabilization (C91, C93) is supported by the structural data and computational simulations (C92), providing converging evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The G966-C1400 interaction is disrupted in frameshifting contexts due to altered base-pairing at the third codon-anticodon position, and genetic suppression data indicates functional coupling between G966 and the P/E loop nucleotide G1338 in maintaining P-site tRNA stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99 provide structural evidence for G966-C1400 disruption in frameshifting contexts (C98) linked to altered codon-anticodon interactions (C96-C97). The genetic suppression data (C100-C101) provides independent functional evidence supporting the structural observations, strengthening the conclusion about the role of these interactions in frame maintenance.

results.result: In frameshifting contexts, the tRNA-mRNA pair moves to an intermediate e*/E position similar to but distinct from EF-G-mediated translocation intermediates, with weakened codon-anticodon interactions that likely reform upon completion of translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107 compare the e*/E position with EF-G-containing translocation intermediates (C103-C104), noting similarities and differences in codon-anticodon bonding distances (C105-C106). The inference about interaction reformation (C107) is reasonable based on the structural comparisons, though it represents a mechanistic interpretation rather than direct observation.

results.result: The m1G37 modification influences tRNAPro-CGG stability on the ribosome and causes large conformational changes of the 30S head domain, but the modification alone does not stabilize the tRNA—rather, stability is heavily influenced by the codon-anticodon interaction context.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 and C4-C5, C61 synthesize the major findings showing that m1G37 presence does not prevent destabilization when slippery codons are present. The structural data from multiple structures (cognate vs. slippery codons, with and without m1G37) provides strong comparative evidence for this conclusion, representing the central mechanistic insight of the study.

results.result: Frameshift-prone tRNAs cause spontaneous head domain swiveling and tilting after occupying the P site, driven by weakened P/E loop and G966-C1400 interactions, which may prevent EF-G binding and lead to increased tRNA dissociation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C115 combine structural observations (C110-C112) with cited smFRET data (C113) and speculations about EF-G binding and tRNA dissociation (C114-C115). While the structural evidence for spontaneous head movement is strong, the predictions about EF-G binding prevention and increased dissociation are speculative and would require additional experimental validation.

results.result: EF-G may have a role in mRNA frame maintenance in addition to its established translocation function, as suggested by its domain IV interactions with tRNA and recent studies showing it can restrict frameshifting on slippery codons.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 are primarily based on cited literature (C116-C118) with a speculative hypothesis (C119). While the cited evidence supports EF-G's potential role in frame maintenance, this represents a hypothesis for future work rather than a conclusion directly supported by the current structural data. Additional experiments would be needed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: Different tRNAPro isoacceptors show varying dependencies on m1G37 and EF-P for frameshift suppression, potentially due to differences in codon-anticodon pairing (cognate vs. near-cognate) and the presence of other modifications like cmo5U34.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C129 are primarily based on cited literature describing different tRNAPro isoacceptors (C121, C124-C125, C128) with speculative mechanistic explanations (C126, C129). While the cited data is relevant context, the mechanistic interpretations connecting the structural findings to these different isoacceptors are speculative and would require additional structural and functional studies for validation.

results.result: Background context on tRNA modifications, m1G37 prevalence and function, frameshifting mechanisms, and ribosome structure establishes the scientific foundation for the study based on prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C24 and C82-C86 provide background information supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These claims establish the known context for the study including m1G37 prevalence (C6-C7, C10), its role in frameshifting (C9, C11, C15-C16), and ribosome structure/function (C22-C23, C83-C84). The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Chemically synthesized ASL and standard ribosome purification methods were used to ensure complete m1G37 modification and obtain functional ribosomes for structural studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 describe methodological approaches supported by appropriate citations (Maehigashi et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2018). These are standard methods appropriately applied to ensure experimental validity, particularly the use of chemically synthesized ASL to guarantee complete modification.
